title: Ceiling fan: safe teardown
summary: Take a ceiling fan down and get its slow outer-rotor motor, the speed capacitor, sealed bearings, switches and light kit; DC fans also give a magnet motor and a driver board. The danger is the ladder and the wiring: switch the circuit off at the breaker, prove it dead, and have a helper for the 8–11 kg lift.

steps.text: Switch the fan off at its wall switch, then switch off its circuit at the breaker or fuse box. Tape over the breaker and the wall switch and leave a note so nobody turns them back on (Lynwood manual, Hunter install, iFixit pull chain; see safety_mains_isolation).
steps.warn: A fan can share a circuit with lights and sockets, and a wall switch may not break every wire. Never trust the wall switch alone. A generator, solar or battery inverter or UPS can keep the wiring live with the grid down: switch those off too (safety_mains_isolation).

steps.text: Check your meter or tester on a known live source now (a working socket on another circuit, or a generator or inverter). Try the fan and its light at the wall switch: nothing should happen. That is only a first check. The real proof is at the wires when the canopy is down (step 6).

Set a stepladder fully open on a firm, level floor, just to one side of the fan so you are not working directly under it. Use a wooden or fibreglass ladder if you have one. Keep three points of contact and don't stand on the top step. Choose a ladder tall enough that the canopy is about chest height, so you never work with your arms overhead. Climb down to move the ladder (OSHA ladders).
steps.warn: A fall from a stepladder can kill or cripple. Have a helper hold the ladder and take each part from you.

steps.text: Let any hot bulbs cool first (iFixit pull chain). Take off the glass shade and the bulbs or LED panel. Glass breaks: hand it down, never drop it. Leave the light kit and its wiring in place for now; you take them off on the ground.

Take the blades off: undo the screws holding each blade bracket to the motor and lift blade and bracket away together (Lynwood manual). This takes weight off and stops a blade catching you or the ladder.

Undo the canopy screws (the cover against the ceiling) and slide it down to show the wiring. With your meter on AC volts (checked on a live source just before, and again afterwards), test between every pair of the bare wire ends and from each one to the earth wire. If the wire connectors hide the ends, check each wire with a non-contact tester first, then undo the connectors by their plastic bodies and meter the ends. You want 0 V everywhere.
steps.warn: If anything reads live, stop. Find the right breaker before you touch any wire.

steps.text: Check how the fan hangs. On downrod fans the ball at the top of the rod sits in a socket or slot in the ceiling bracket, so the fan hangs on its own while you work; the Axon's ball twists to seat, so turn it back to free it (Axon guide). Hugger fans hang on a hook on the bracket and are also held by locknuts or locking screws (three 1/4 in locknuts on the Lynwood, two locking screws on Hunter's low-profile fans). Have your helper hold the motor up while you undo them, then leave it hanging on the hook (Hunter install, Lynwood manual). Some remote fans have a receiver sitting in the bracket: unplug its connector to the fan (Axon guide, Hunter fix). The Altura's wiring steps join the fan wires straight to the house wires (Altura DC guide), so look for its receiver inside the fan instead.
Photograph the wiring, then undo the wire connectors and separate the fan wires from the house wires. Put a connector on each house wire, tape it, and fold the wires back into the box.

Lift the fan off: have your helper take hold of the motor housing first. Then free the ball from the bracket (or lift the motor bracket off the hook), holding the motor housing or the downrod, never the wires. Your helper lowers it to the floor; you never carry it down the ladder. A hugger fan sits close to the ceiling, so the helper may need a second stepladder (Hunter install).
steps.warn: The Lynwood weighs 7.7 kg and the Altura 10.8 kg (17 and 23.8 lb) (Lynwood manual, Altura DC guide); yours may weigh more. Don't take the weight alone above your shoulders. Keep your body centred on the steps, don't lean out, and never reach out to catch a slipping fan.

steps.text: On the ground, take the light kit off: undo its screws, free it from the switch cup, and unplug its connector or undo its wire connectors (Lynwood manual). Keep the kit and its wires together.

On the ground, open the switch housing under the motor: undo the cap nut where the chains come out, then the screws around its rim. Inside are the pull-chain switches, the reversing switch and, on AC fans, the capacitor block (iFixit pull chain, Lynwood manual, Hunter fix). Don't touch anything inside until the capacitor is discharged in the next step.

Discharge the capacitor before you touch its terminals: hold the resistor tool across its common wire and each other wire in turn, then measure DC volts (see safety_discharge_capacitor). Write down which colour went to which switch terminal, then cut or unplug the leads.
steps.warn: A fan capacitor can keep a charge from the mains after power is off. Discharge and measure every time.

steps.text: DC fans: find the driver board (in the bracket with the receiver, or inside the motor housing: if it is inside, open the housing first, see the next step). Measure DC volts across its largest capacitors and discharge anything over about 30 V before you unplug the board and lift it out.
steps.warn: A mains driver board can hold about 170 V DC (120 V countries) or 340 V DC (230 V countries) after switch-off.

steps.text: Decide whether to open the motor. How it comes apart varies by model: if screws round the rim join the two halves, undo them and lift the top half off the shaft. If there are no screws, keep the motor whole. On a DC fan the rotor's magnets pull toward the stator, so keep your fingers out of the gap as the halves part.

Test the motor (see test_motor). AC motor: measure each winding and check that no wire reads to the metal case. DC motor: spin the outer shell by hand with the meter on AC volts between two of its motor wires; a reading that rises with speed means magnets and windings are good.

notes:
## Before you strip it

A working fan may be worth more as a fan: moving air keeps people cool in a heatwave. DC fans use far less power. The Altura 68 DC draws 3, 11 and 32 W on its three speeds (Altura DC guide); the Lynwood 52 AC fan draws 10, 27 and 62 W (Lynwood manual). LBNL's estimate is that swapping an induction motor for a brushless one cuts a fan's power use by about half (LBNL fans). A DC fan is the one to run from a solar battery through an inverter.

## What's worth keeping and why

- **AC motor.** A single-phase induction motor (TI BLDC fan, DOE fan rule) whose outer shell spins with the blades. It is slow: 65–185 rpm on the Lynwood (Lynwood manual). Keep its capacitor with it; most fans use the capacitor to set the speed steps (Hunter fix). It runs only on mains AC. Don't feed it from a lamp dimmer or other solid-state speed control: the Lynwood manual warns this can cause fire or shock. It is not a generator: an induction motor gives nothing out when you spin it (see test_motor).
- **DC (brushless) motor.** A permanent-magnet motor driven by an electronic board (DOE fan rule), often three-phase (TI BLDC fan). Because it has magnets, spinning the outer shell makes AC, so it is a candidate for a slow wind or water generator with a rectifier. Output varies a lot by model: test before you build around it. To use it as a motor again, keep it with its own driver board.
- **Driver board (DC fans).** Converts mains to DC and drives the motor (TI BLDC fan). Keep it with its motor and remote; parts alone are of little use.
- **Capacitor block.** A film capacitor, often with several sections in one can. The pull-chain switch picks sections to change speed. If a fan only runs on high, the capacitor may be bad (Hunter fix). Record the microfarad (µF) and voltage values printed on it; it is a spare for another fan with the same values.
- **Bearings.** Permanently lubricated sealed ball bearings (Lynwood manual, Altura DC guide). Good for slow-turning shafts: a turntable, a wind vane, a small cart axle.
- **Switches.** The pull-chain speed switch (on the Lynwood: one pull high, two medium, three low, four off), the light pull chain and the slide reversing switch (Lynwood manual). A pull-chain switch makes a light switch you can work from below.
- **Light kit.** LED panels or bulb sockets with their wiring. The Lynwood takes two candelabra bulbs of up to 60 W each (Lynwood manual). LED panels run on mains through their own driver.
- **Remote and receiver.** Keep them together: they are paired by matching DIP switches, and the Axon remote takes an A23 12 V battery (Axon guide).
- **Downrod, bracket, screws and short wires.**

## Variations

- **Hampton Bay Lynwood 52 (52-LWD):** AC, two pull chains, a reversing switch in the switch cup, two candelabra sockets, five blades, and a hugger mount that hangs on a hook while you wire it. 7.7 kg (17.0 lb) net (Lynwood manual).
- **Home Decorators Axon 52 (52-AXON):** remote control, a receiver that sits in the ceiling bracket on top of the downrod ball and plugs into the motor through a moulded connector, and a light kit with three colour temperatures (Axon guide).
- **Home Decorators Altura 68 DC (68-ATRDC):** DC motor with remote. At start-up it oscillates back and forth during a calibration cycle; the guide says this is normal. 10.8 kg (23.81 lb) net, on a box rated for 22.7 kg (50 lb) (Altura DC guide).
- Downrod fans hang by a ball and tab in the bracket (Altura DC guide, Hunter install); hugger fans sit tight to the ceiling.
- Not every AC fan has a capacitor: LBNL notes shaded-pole fan motors too (LBNL fans).

## What to leave

- The ceiling box and house wiring. Leave them in place with each wire capped and taped.
- The DC rotor's magnets. Leave them in the shell; you need them in place to use the motor as a generator.
- Cracked glass shades and decorative housings, unless you need the glass.

## Testing what you got out

- **Capacitor:** after discharging, read it on a meter's capacitance range if it has one and compare with the printed values.
- **Switches:** use the continuity range and click through each position.
- **Motors:** see the last step and test_motor.
